author: Sigmund Freud
biz: Ask what the money is actually for

The gap between manifest and latent is a Consumer Duty tool as much as a sales one. An enquiry that says consolidate my debts can mean a new kitchen or a court date, and the two need different outcomes. This week, add one open question near the start of every HomeownersLoan call, along the lines of what would have to change for this to feel sorted, and require the answer in the notes before any product talk. Measure the share of cases with that field completed, and watch whether suitability referrals and later complaints move. No steering, just the real need written down.
Stop killing channels on a single cause

Dreams, Freud found, are overdetermined, with one image resting on several thoughts at once. Lead sources behave the same way. A Facebook impression, a brand search on Bing and an organic page can all be necessary for one funded Apply4Loan case, while last click credit goes only to the last of them. This week, pull a conversion path report over ninety days and count how many funded cases touched more than one source. Measure assisted conversions beside cost per funded case, and pause nothing on last click alone.

b: Sigmund Freud was born on the sixth of May 1856, in rented rooms above a locksmith's shop in Freiberg in Moravia, a small market town in the Austrian Empire that is now Pribor in the Czech Republic. His father Jakob was a wool merchant, forty years old, and already a grandfather. His mother Amalia was twenty one. The arithmetic of that household mattered more to the boy than anyone in it could have guessed.

Jakob had two grown sons from an earlier marriage, Emanuel and Philipp. Emanuel had children of his own, so the new baby had a nephew his own age and a mother younger than his half brothers. A small child working out who belonged to whom in that flat had a genuine puzzle on his hands, and the question of which man is the father and which the rival is one he would spend his life returning to.

The wool trade failed. In 1859 the family left for Leipzig, and in 1860 they settled in Vienna, where Freud would live for the next seventy eight years. Money was short, the flats were small, and the eldest boy was the hope of the house. He was given a room of his own for his books. When his sister's piano practice disturbed him, the piano was removed.

There was also a nursemaid in Freiberg, an elderly Catholic woman who took him to church and told him about heaven and hell, and who was dismissed after Philipp had her prosecuted for stealing from the household. Freud was about two and a half. He only recovered the memory in his forties, while picking his own childhood apart in letters to a friend in Berlin, and he wrote about her with the particular attention of a man who had just worked out that nothing is ever simply forgotten.

b: He entered the University of Vienna in 1873 to read medicine, without much loving it. What he loved was looking at a thing through a microscope until it gave up its structure. In 1876 his teacher Carl Claus sent him to the zoological station at Trieste with a question that had defeated naturalists for centuries. Nobody had ever found the testes of the eel.

Freud dissected about four hundred eels over several weeks. He found tissue that might have been what he was looking for, and he could not prove it. His report was careful and inconclusive, and the problem was settled by other people later. He had learned two things that outlasted the eels. The first was that a hidden structure can be entirely real and still refuse to show itself. The second was how to keep cutting.

From 1877 he worked in Ernst Brucke's physiology laboratory, six years of the most rigorous science in Europe, staining nerve cells, counting, drawing. Brucke's view of a living body was that it is a system of forces in which energy is conserved and must go somewhere. Freud never stopped thinking that way. When he later wrote about a wish being dammed up and finding another outlet, he was writing physiology in a borrowed language.

He qualified as a doctor of medicine in March 1881, three years later than his contemporaries, because he had been enjoying the laboratory too much to leave it. He had no money and no prospect of a chair. Brucke, who liked him, told him plainly to give up a research career he could not afford.

b: In April 1882 he met Martha Bernays at his family's flat. He was twenty six, she was twenty one, and they were engaged within months. The engagement then lasted more than four years, because he had nothing to marry on. That is the pressure under which he did the worst work of his life.

In 1884 he published a paper called On Coca, praising cocaine with an enthusiasm that reads badly now. He saw two uses. One was as a local anaesthetic, which he mentioned and did not pursue. His colleague Karl Koller took that same observation to the eye clinic, demonstrated the first local anaesthetic in surgery, and became famous that year. The other use was as a cure for morphine addiction. Freud recommended cocaine to his friend and colleague Ernst von Fleischl-Marxow, who was taking morphine for unbearable pain in an amputated thumb. Fleischl became one of the first recorded cocaine addicts in Europe and died in 1891.

Freud had taken leave to visit Martha when the anaesthetic discovery was made in Vienna without him. He mentions it afterwards without much self pity, but the double lesson was expensive. He had been right about something and had not done the work, and he had been confidently wrong about something else, and a friend had paid for it.
It is worth holding on to this before anything else in his life, because the man who later wrote about self deception was not a stranger to his own. He knew exactly what it feels like to be sure.
ch.cap: A lost prize and a friend he could not save

b: In October 1885 he travelled to Paris on a fellowship, to the Salpetriere hospital, to watch Jean-Martin Charcot. Charcot was the most celebrated neurologist in Europe, and in his Tuesday demonstrations he did something that changed Freud's mind about what counts as an illness. He took hysteria seriously.

Patients arrived with paralysed arms, with blindness, with fits and contractures, and with no damage anywhere that a doctor could find. They were not dismissed as frauds. Charcot showed that their symptoms followed rules, that they could be produced and removed again under hypnosis, and therefore that they were caused by ideas. An idea could paralyse an arm. Freud, trained to hunt for damaged nerve tissue, was watching a symptom that had a meaning.

He came home in 1886, married Martha in a civil ceremony on the thirteenth of September, and opened a private practice treating nervous disorders. In 1891 the family moved to Berggasse 19, where he would see patients for the next forty seven years, and where the famous couch, a gift from a grateful patient, eventually arrived.

Then came the ordinary problem of a working practice. Hypnosis did not do what Charcot's demonstrations promised, Freud was not especially good at it, and there were people in the room every day who needed something from him.

b: His older colleague Josef Breuer had a story worth hearing. From 1880 to 1882 he had treated a young woman he called Anna O., whose real name was Bertha Pappenheim, and had found that her symptoms eased when she described in detail the circumstances in which each one had first appeared. She called it the talking cure.

Freud began with pressure and suggestion, laying a hand on the patient's forehead and insisting that a memory would come. Then, gradually, he took himself out of the procedure. If he said nothing, asked nothing and forbade nothing, and simply required the patient to report every thought that arrived, however trivial, irrelevant or embarrassing, the material came anyway. Better than that, it came in chains.

That is free association, and it is the most consequential technique he ever invented. Its logic is severe. If you let a mind wander under instruction not to censor itself, the direction it wanders in is not random. Something is pulling the chain.

In 1895 he and Breuer published Studies on Hysteria. In the same year, over a few hot weeks, Freud wrote a draft he never published, an attempt to describe the whole mind as a system of neurones and quantities of excitation. He abandoned it. The machine he wanted did not exist yet. So he did the thing that makes the rest of this story. He went looking for a single specimen he could take all the way down.

b: That summer the family was staying at Bellevue, a house on a hill outside Vienna. Two months earlier Freud had sent a patient, Emma Eckstein, to his friend Wilhelm Fliess in Berlin for an operation on her nose, which Fliess believed could cure neurotic symptoms. Fliess left surgical gauze in the wound. Emma Eckstein nearly bled to death and was left permanently disfigured.

On the night of the twenty third of July, Freud dreamed about a patient he called Irma. In the dream he reproaches her for not accepting his solution, she complains of pain, he looks into her throat and sees white patches and scabs, a Doctor M. pronounces it an infection, and the infection is traced back to an injection given by another colleague with a dirty syringe. Nobody in the dream is to blame except other people.

Freud spent weeks on it, and became the first person to take a single dream apart completely, image by image, writing down for each one every association that occurred to him. What he found underneath the anxiety was a defence. The dream argued, with the ingenuity of a good barrister, that the illness was not his fault and his treatment was not at fault either. The wish was to be innocent. The dream granted it.

From that he took the general claim. A dream is not a prophecy and not a meaningless nerve storm. A dream is the fulfilment of a wish, and the strange surface you remember, the manifest content, is a disguised version of a latent content underneath it. Years later, on the twelfth of June 1900, he wrote to Fliess asking whether a marble tablet might one day be fixed to that house, saying that in it, on the twenty fourth of July 1895, the secret of dreams was revealed to Doctor Sigmund Freud. Then he answered himself. The prospects, he thought, looked slim.
ch.cap: The first dream taken apart completely
ch.when: Bellevue, outside Vienna, the night of the twenty third of July 1895

b: Jakob Freud died on the twenty third of October 1896. His son wrote later that the death of the father is the most important event and the most poignant loss in a man's life. It opened something. For the next three years Freud analysed his own dreams night after night, and most of the dreams in the book that followed are his own.

Two letters from 1897 mark the turn. On the twenty first of September he wrote to Fliess that he no longer believed in his neurotica, abandoning his theory that every case of hysteria rested on a real seduction in childhood. On the fifteenth of October he described what he thought replaced it, having found in himself love for the mother and jealousy of the father, and he named it after Sophocles.

Both letters are still fought over. The abandonment has been read as intellectual honesty, and by Jeffrey Masson in 1984 as a loss of nerve that turned real abuse into fantasy. What matters for the dream book is the method that produced them. Freud was now treating his own mind as the specimen, and his own reluctance as evidence.

Out of those three years came the machinery. A dream is built from the day's residues, the odd leftover impressions of waking life, harnessed to a much older wish. A censor stands between the wish and the sleeping mind, and the wish gets past it only by being transformed. Several thoughts are compressed into one image, which he called condensation. Feeling is detached from what matters and attached to something trivial, which is displacement. The result is staged as a scene rather than argued as a sentence. Then, on waking, it is tidied into a story that almost makes sense, which he called secondary revision.
ch.cap: Three years analysing his own nights

b: He wrote the book across 1898 and 1899, rewriting the chapter on the dream work again and again. Franz Deuticke published it in Vienna on the fourth of November 1899 and put 1900 on the title page, which is how a book about the hidden life of the mind acquired the right date by accident.

Its argument runs in a straight line. Dreams have meaning. The meaning is a wish. The wish is usually old and usually unacceptable, so it is disguised by the dream work. Dreams therefore guard sleep, discharging in disguise what would otherwise wake the sleeper. And because the same disguises turn up in symptoms, in jokes and in slips of the tongue, a dream is the ordinary person's nightly proof that most of mental life happens out of sight. The interpretation of dreams, he wrote, is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.

The last chapter is the one specialists still read. In it he stops talking about dreams and sketches the apparatus that produces them, with a primary process that knows no time, no contradiction and no negation, and a secondary process that does the delaying and the reality testing. Regression is his name for the route by which a thought, blocked from reaching action, travels backwards until it turns into a picture.

Deuticke printed six hundred copies. It took eight years to sell them. There were few reviews and several were poor. Freud was forty three, and the book that now appears on every list of the century's most important had, for the better part of a decade, almost no readers at all.

b: It came good slowly. Young doctors in Zurich read it, Carl Jung among them, and it became the entry text for a movement. Freud revised it for seven further editions, the last in 1929, and in the preface to the third English edition in 1931 he called it the most valuable of all the discoveries it had been his good fortune to make, adding that insight such as that falls to one's lot but once in a lifetime. He left Vienna on the fourth of June 1938, after the Anschluss, and died in London on the twenty third of September 1939.

Then the science moved. In 1953 rapid eye movement sleep was identified in a Chicago laboratory, and dreaming turned out to run on a biological clock that no wish could have set. In 1977 Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley proposed activation synthesis, in which dreaming begins with signals rising from the brain stem and the forebrain simply makes the best story it can out of the noise. On that account the strangeness of dreams needs no censor at all, because there was never anything being hidden.

The argument has not stopped. In 1997 and 2000 Mark Solms, working with brain injured patients who had stopped dreaming altogether, located dreaming in forebrain systems rather than the brain stem and argued that it is driven by a motivational circuit, which he took as partial support for Freud. Karl Popper objected that the theory explained everything and forbade nothing. Hans Eysenck argued in 1985 that Freud's own dreams refuted him. Max Schur argued in 1972 that the Irma dream was Freud shielding Fliess and himself from what had happened to Emma Eckstein, which would make the founding specimen of the method the clearest demonstration of it.

What survived is not the dream dictionary. It is the structure. That mental life is mostly unconscious and active rather than merely stored, that symptoms and errors carry meaning, that the way to reach any of it is to let somebody talk without steering them, and that a mind spends a great deal of its energy keeping things from itself. Every consulting room that works by listening is somewhere on the road he named.

Nietzsche had already described forgetting as an active achievement rather than a failure, which is Freud's censor in philosophical dress, and Freud always insisted he had come to him late and reluctantly.

note: The life is drawn from The Interpretation of Dreams itself, from Freud's letters to Wilhelm Fliess, and from standard biographical accounts including those of Ernest Jones and Peter Gay. The publication details, the dating of the Irma dream to the night of the twenty third of July 1895 and the marble tablet letter of the twelfth of June 1900 follow the published correspondence and the Standard Edition. Several episodes here are disputed: the identity of the patient called Irma, how far the nursemaid memory can be trusted, and above all Max Schur's reading of the dream as self exculpation over Emma Eckstein, which is an interpretation and not Freud's own account. Jeffrey Masson's 1984 attack on the abandoned seduction theory, and the Hobson, Solms and Popper objections in the last chapter, are given as the live arguments they still are, and no dialogue has been invented.
recall: On what night did Freud dream the dream of Irma's injection, and why is that dream the centre of the book?

He dreamed it at Bellevue, outside Vienna, on the night of the twenty third of July 1895. It was the first dream he took apart completely, association by association, and it gave him his general claim that a dream is the disguised fulfilment of a wish. The wish in this one was to be innocent of a patient's suffering.
What are the operations of the dream work?

Condensation, where several thoughts are compressed into one image. Displacement, where feeling is moved off what matters on to something trivial. Staging, where a thought becomes a visual scene rather than a sentence. And secondary revision, where the mind tidies the result into a story that almost makes sense.
What happened to Emma Eckstein, and why does it matter to the Irma dream?

In 1895 Freud sent her to Wilhelm Fliess for nasal surgery. Fliess left surgical gauze in the wound, she nearly bled to death and was left disfigured. Max Schur argued in 1972 that the Irma dream was Freud absolving Fliess and himself of that disaster, which would make the founding example of the method a demonstration of it.
When was The Interpretation of Dreams published, and how did it sell?

Franz Deuticke published it in Vienna on the fourth of November 1899, with 1900 printed on the title page. The run was six hundred copies and it took eight years to sell them. Freud then revised it for seven further editions, the last in 1929.
What did Hobson and McCarley propose in 1977, and why does it threaten Freud?

Their activation synthesis hypothesis held that dreaming begins with signals rising from the brain stem, which the forebrain then assembles into the best story it can manage. If the strangeness of a dream is noise rather than disguise, you need no censor and no hidden wish to explain it.
recap:
Sigmund Freud was born on the sixth of May 1856 in rented rooms above a locksmith's shop in Freiberg in Moravia. His father Jakob was a wool merchant of forty with two grown sons already, and his mother Amalia was twenty one. The wool trade failed, and by 1860 the family was in Vienna, poor, with the eldest boy as its hope.

He was a laboratory scientist before he was anything else. In 1876 he dissected about four hundred eels at Trieste looking for organs nobody had ever found, and failed honestly. From 1877 he spent six years in Ernst Brucke's physiology laboratory, learning to see a living body as a system of forces in which energy must go somewhere.

Then he was expensively wrong. His 1884 paper on cocaine gave the local anaesthetic away to Karl Koller and recommended the drug to his friend Ernst von Fleischl-Marxow, who became an addict and died in 1891. The man who later wrote about self deception knew from the inside what certainty feels like.

In Paris, in the winter of 1885 to 1886, he watched Charcot take hysteria seriously and prove that an idea could paralyse an arm. He married Martha Bernays in September 1886, opened a practice, and moved to Berggasse 19 in 1891. Hypnosis failed him, so he removed himself from the procedure and asked patients only to report every thought without censoring it. That is free association.

On the night of the twenty third of July 1895, at Bellevue outside Vienna, he dreamed about a patient he called Irma. Two months earlier he had sent Emma Eckstein to Wilhelm Fliess for nasal surgery that nearly killed her. The dream argued, elaborately, that nobody involved was at fault. Taking it apart gave him his claim. A dream is the disguised fulfilment of a wish.

His father died in October 1896, and three years of self analysis followed. The machinery came with it. The leftover impressions of the day are harnessed to a much older wish, and a censor forces that wish through condensation, displacement, staging and secondary revision, which is why what you remember makes so little sense. Dreams guard sleep.

Deuticke published the book on the fourth of November 1899 with 1900 on the cover. Six hundred copies, eight years to sell them. Since then rapid eye movement sleep, Hobson and McCarley's activation synthesis and Popper's objection have taken most of the theory apart, while Solms has handed some of it back. The method outlived the claims.

Most of your mind is working without telling you, and the only way in is to let it talk.
stories: Four hundred eels and nothing to show

In 1876, aged twenty, Freud was sent to the zoological station at Trieste with a question that had beaten naturalists for centuries. Nobody had found the testes of the eel. He dissected about four hundred of them over several weeks, found tissue that might have been the answer, and could not prove it. His report was careful and inconclusive. He got no discovery out of that summer, but he got the habit that made him, which is that a hidden structure can be entirely real and still refuse for years to show itself to anybody unwilling to keep cutting.

In 1884 Freud published a paper praising cocaine, noting in passing that it numbed the tissue it touched. Then he took leave to visit his fiancee Martha. While he was away his colleague Karl Koller carried that same observation into the eye clinic, demonstrated the first local anaesthetic in surgery, and became famous that year. Meanwhile Freud had been recommending cocaine to cure his friend Ernst von Fleischl-Marxow of morphine addiction. Fleischl became one of Europe's first cocaine addicts and died in 1891. One idea given away, one pushed much too far.
The tablet that was never fixed to the wall

On the twelfth of June 1900 Freud wrote to Wilhelm Fliess about the house at Bellevue where, five years earlier, he had dreamed about the patient he called Irma. He asked whether a marble tablet might one day be placed on it, reading that in this house, on the twenty fourth of July 1895, the secret of dreams was revealed to Doctor Sigmund Freud. Then he answered his own question. The prospects, he thought, looked slim. His book had sold a few dozen copies. There is no tablet, and the house itself is long gone.
take: Treat an odd, outsized reaction as information about something older rather than about the thing in front of you. Ask what it reminds you of before you ask whether it is reasonable.
The surface is the disguise, not the message
When a stated reason is unusually tidy, go looking for the version that is less flattering. In your own motives and in everybody else's, the account you can describe is the edited one.
Stop steering and the material arrives
The fastest way to find what somebody actually wants is one open question and then silence for longer than is comfortable. Interrupt and all you get back is your own hypothesis.

Freud found that a single dream image usually sat on top of many thoughts at once. Most outcomes you care about are like that, so if you remove only the first cause you find, the thing tends to happen again.
Certainty is a feeling, not evidence
He was at his most confidently wrong where he had most at stake. Before committing, write down what would have to be true and what would change your mind.
A defence is doing a job
When someone resists an obvious conclusion, the resistance is protecting something. Find out what, before you try to argue it away, because the argument will lose.
Almost all of Freud's content has been revised or abandoned and his procedure is still in daily use. Build the way you investigate with more care than the conclusions, because it will survive them.
Work one specimen all the way down
He made his case by taking a single dream apart completely rather than many superficially. One case worked to the bottom teaches more than fifty summaries.
title: The Night He Took His Own Dream Apart
wiifm: You will come away able to say what Freud actually claimed, which is narrower and stranger than the version everybody repeats. You will know what the dream work is, how a wish gets past a censor, and why he thought a dream protects your sleep rather than disturbing it. You will hear how a man who had already been expensively wrong about cocaine built a method out of his own worst night. And you will know where a century of sleep science has broken his theory and where it has not, so you can use the half of it that still works.

A Freudian dream is a palimpsest, with a childhood wish showing faintly through the leftover impressions of the day.
